comments.body:
This should’ve been a season of For All Mankind, the alternate-history series that imagines what might have happened if the space race had never ended. Except on that show, they probably would’ve figured this out by the ’90s. By the millennium, they already had a colony on Mars and had moved on to problems like robotics replacing human workers—all fueled by the same old forces of ambition, competition, and greed.

It’s difficult to say whether life is imitating art or the other way around. Either way, with Russia, China, and the United States racing to be first, the parallels are hard to miss. But putting nuclear reactors on the Moon isn’t a contest where failure means losing a trophy or falling behind. When national prestige and geopolitical rivalry start dictating the timetable, mistakes can have consequences that extend far beyond a single mission. Something will eventually go wrong, and the resulting “bump on the learning curve” could be catastrophic.

Ironically, it may take exactly that kind of disaster to remind these superpowers that space—and the technologies we bring there—should demand cooperation rather than another arms race. Perhaps then they’ll work together for the betterment of all mankind.

In 1979, the United Nations drafted an international agreement dealing with the moon's exploration. Its Article VII reads, in part,  "In exploring and using the moon, States Parties shall take measures to prevent the disruption of the existing balance of its environment, whether by introducing adverse changes in that environment, by its harmful contamination through the introduction of extra-environmental matter or otherwise."
Unfortunately, because of vagueness in some of its provisions, according to Wikipedia, "It has not been ratified by any state that engages in self-launched human spaceflight (i.e., the United States, Russia (or its predecessor the Soviet Union), or the People's Republic of China) since its creation on December 18, 1979, and thus it has little to no relevancy in international law."
A nuclear accident involving reactors on the moon thus might not have any consequences beyond further damaging the ecosystem there (already a junkyard littered with failed landers, rocket parts and astronauts' abandoned equipment.)

It is their fault that no such law exists. The ruling was constitutionally correct even if half the country doesn’t like the fact. 

On mail-in voting, the constitution is clear. States determine the conducting of elections. Any change in that from the federal level would require an amendment to the constitution. Entire states use only mail-in voting. (There’s a different legal concern regarding whether this itself is constitutional as it disenfranchises those who don’t trust the mail system and demand to vote in person). 

The court’s record is nonpartisan. You may not like this ruling or that one, but the constitution is supreme, above party and politic.

Compulsivity turns into an illness only if it interferes with the rest of one's life, such as double and triple checking everything, various rites that must be performed to prevent increased anxiety and so on. 

The same is true with many other factors in life. It's not so much that they exist, but the extent to which they exist, whether they coexist with other factors that increase the anxiety or interference of one's life. Call it the "p" factor if you like. The concept is not new, just the label.

For many years, I developed and managed dual diagnosis (addiction/mental health) evening treatment programs and related services.  I am a professional counselor who was certified in both fields. 

Psychiatric labels are useful mostly as a sort of shorthand language to describe the most salient features of a person's mental illness. But all too often, in my experience, they are handed out like candy. Don't like this one? Then let's try that one. 

In treatment, I've found it's more helpful to ignore labels and focus on the person's current needs, whether they are to become sober and clean, to improve psychosocial relationships or to overcome various symptoms such as depressed or elevated mood or anxiety.  

I have found some professionals all too eager to change diagnoses, especially those made by others, without a clear understanding of the circumstances. 

For example, a woman with a long term diagnosis of depression told a new doctor that her boyfriend said that she talked too fast. On this basis alone diagnosed her as having bipolar disorder. She did not have bipolar disorder. She had a boyfriend from the Deep South who was accustomed to a slower manner of speaking.  The medication he gave her caused serious side effects. When she stopped that medication and returned to her former medication, those side effects went away. She never exhibited symptoms of bipolar disorder at all. The doctor did not consider all of the elements of a possible diagnosis.

Reading about the Renault reminded me of an incident with my own car when I first moved to NYC. I won’t divulge the details, because it’s a story I’ve meant to work up for the Met Diary myself.

I mention it because, speaking only for myself, some stories take a lot of work to reach a level of quality that this column deserves. And some stories deserve a place in the Diary. The hilarious Renault piece is one of those gems.

Myself, I recast some stories dozens of times, sometimes for years. It doesn’t come easy for me. When they reach a point where I’m super pleased, I let them sit for a week or two. And invariably, what thrilled me one day, often reveals patches that suddenly strike me as clumsy, inartful, unclear or just requiring another level of polish. Then the process begins again.

I looked through my archives today and found a draft of that story about my car. Ugh! I hated it! Really hokey. It will be some time before I even attempt another rewrite.

For you writers out there, you have a lifetime of New York stories that deserve to be polished into gold. I encourage you to work on them, sleep on them, and polish them until they shine. It’s okay to hold them back until they do. But do make them shine, and send them in to the Diary. And never let a few unsuccessful submissions stop you from sending more. Just keep trying.

— Paul

I and my wife were living in Pataya, Thailand in 1968-9, where I was stationed in the U S Army (drafted in 1968).  We travelled as much as we could on days/weeks off.

Ah, the memories…we left Bangkok with galvanized tubs of ice filled with bottles of Singha beer and open windows drawing in the warm, humid air from the countryside .  After a bit of time, we were drinking lukewarm beer, as the ice had melted.  And to test our balance, we used the “restroom” car, which necessitated one’s crouching above the hole in the floor and aiming, seeing the train tracks below.  

We did the funicular train ride, also, which I thought was very cool (having grown up in Oklahoma). Loved the life in the city, the morning sound of the call to prayers, everything so exotic to us.

On New Year’s Eve, 1969, we went as guests to a party at the Chinese Swimming Club where the band played “Oklahoma hills”…how weird was that!

Fun piece here for me.  Thank you.

"Skydance will need to find tens of millions of new subscribers to catch up to Netflix, Amazon and Disney in the streaming wars."

This is the biggest hurdle of all. Netflix' global growth has been stalling lately, a sign that the industry as a whole is reaching saturation. Now comes the period of consolidation as the stronger contenders draw way the weaker streamers' customers. The stronger ones are Netflix, Amazon and Disney. Not HBO Max or Paramount+.

Netflix subscribers don't tend to churn. Paramount+ and HBO Max both have higher churn. They can trot out some buzzy new show but then the churners will binge watch and bail. 

They can pay out the wazoo for pricey sports, but that's a double-edged sword. Netflix grew into a behemoth while ignoring sports and still only dabbles. A lot of subscribers don't want to subsidize sports they never watch. Price increases to cover sports will increase churn among the already churn-prone.

Good luck to Ellison but I don't think he knows what he's doing. The streaming wars are over and Netflix won. Now we wants to jump into a war that's winding down? The next war is the AI war and Netflix and Disney are both gearing up for that. Pretty soon Ellison will realize a different war is raging, that he hasn't prepared for in the least. The classic problem of generals planning to fight the last war.

comments.name: George
comments.body:
A classic case of confusion needs with wants.

I find it fascinating to read how many here oppose banning a product that results in such deleterious health risks for workers engaged in preparing it.

Firstly, of course, no one, absolutely no one, needs a quartz countertop.  One may like quartz countertops and one may want a quartz countertop, but no one needs one.

Moreover, there are fine substitutes available such as granite and marble, as well as good old formica, which provide the same decorative benefits as do quartz countertops.

So, in a sense, whilst confusing wants with needs we see people engaging in a moral quandary.

If the preparation of a quartz countertop raises the risk of debilitating disease and death while the preparation of an alternative doesn't, then is it not incumbent upon us to favor the safe alternative and ban the unsafe one?

Yes, workers could be required to wear masks, albeit we know they probably won't.

So, knowing the very real risks to production workers of a product; and knowing that fine substitute alternatives exist; why is it so hard to rise to the level of simple decency and ban the bad while embracing the good?

It wasn't the oil and auto industries who built all the highways.  It was the government--the government we elected--that built the roads.  And they were seen as great improvements back then.  Back then, Natl Geo did a big feature on the wonders of the new Interstate Highway System.

But the highway push goes back further.  New York City had a good network of clean fast electric streetcars, many routes using the latest models.  But Mayor LaGuardia didn't like trolleys and ordered them all converted to buses, which they were.

Further, Mayor LaGuardia appointed Robert Moses who pushed through a massive network of highways and bridges in and around NYC.

In Washington DC, they had a nice streetcar network and the company was happy running trolleys.  But Congress wanted them killed off and they were.

Many town governments pushed to convert fast electric streets to slow noisy buses in the name of "progress".  Point is that it was the town that pushed for this, not industry.

There is something almost allegorical about Jeff Koons owning a $100 million collection of Picasso, Manet and Dutch masters. Koons has been one of the great beneficiaries of an art market that converts provocation, branding and irony into immense private wealth. That wealth, in turn, allowed him to buy works by artists whose ambitions and achievements seem vastly greater than his own.

One needn’t deny Koons’s ingenuity, technical polish or importance to contemporary art to wonder what social or artistic value justifies the extraordinary sums attached to his work. A $91 million stainless-steel rabbit did not become culturally important because it cost $91 million; rather, the price became part of the work’s aura and importance. Meanwhile, the artist who made it could use the proceeds of that system to acquire Manet and Picasso.

Perhaps that is the most successful Koons work of all: an art-market system in which the joke about value became valuable enough to buy the real thing.

We left Italy (Milan) a month ago.  My wife was waffling about making purchases in two different stores when the sales clerks offered that she was entitled to a VAT refund if she had her passport on her.  She called me (several shops away), I returned and the clerks filled out all the paperwork.

They gave us forms for Global Blue and told us how to scan them at the airport (MXP).  We found the location, used a self serve kiosk, scanned the provided documents and received a message that our refund was approved.  Within two weeks I saw the refund on my American Express statement.

This could not have been any easier.  Buy, scan, refund.   The old days of standing in line to get a stamp and mailing receipts are coming to an end.

My family moved from the US to Brazil in 1988. My parents were sent as Catholic lay missioners to work with the poor. The dictatorship had ended a few years before and Jose Sarney was chosen as president. The first free elections were held in 1990: Lula vs Collor. Collor won. I remember kids at my school saying their parents couldn't vote for Lula, because if he won there would be homeless people sleeping at our school. The fear of the left has always been there. Collor was impeached in 1992 after several corruption schemes came to light. Lula was finally elected in 2003. He's been around forever, and Brazil has experienced several corruption scandals since. Who does the PT have to take the reigns? Where's the next generation. Dark times indeed as the global shift to the right will probably lead to the destruction of the Amazon.

The early 90s was an interesting time in Brazil. The country had a plebiscite election in 1993 (following Collor's impeachment) to decide on the form and system of government. Republic and Presidentialism won overwhelmingly. The ads calling for a return to a monarchy is something I'll never forget though. 'Vote no Rei' (vote for the King).

The unfolding ebola outbreak highlights a mounting public health crisis shaped by shifting climatic patterns and erratic weather extremes that alter ecological boundaries. 

As prolonged droughts and rising temperatures disrupt natural forest habitats and food sources, reservoir hosts like fruit bats are forced to migrate and forage closer to human agricultural settlements. 

This heightened overlap intensifies human-wildlife interaction, while concurrent pressures on local food security elevate the reliance on bushmeat. 

Ultimately, climate-driven environmental degradation amplifies the risk of novel viral transmission, compounding the vulnerabilities that fuel modern epidemics.

comments.body: Cider is one of my favorite low ABV drinks. Usually half the alcohol of wine, and more refreshing for me than beer, a nice Normandy or heritage breed northeast cider is one of the finest beverages.  And ranging from bone-dry to off-dry, they are incredibly easy to pair with food. While there are lots of expensive bottled ciders on the market, some of basic cans are still a great deal, such as Downeast or Hudson.

comments.name: Steve
comments.body: I am sorry to hear of his passing; I was not familiar with his work. In the 1980s, I lived in the Swabian part of Germany, and nearly every family with a yard had an apple tree. It was an annual tradition to take the apple harvest every year to a centuries-old water mill, crush the fruit, and then begin the process of fermenting the juice into hard cider (Moscht). During the winter months, a glass of Moscht was a staple during the evening meal. Everyone had a barrel in the garage or basement. This inspired me earlier this year to start making it in our own home, where we now have it available most of the time. It is incredibly easy, inexpensive, and the results are astoundingly good. I guess I can credit Mr. Watson for inspiring all the online videos I consulted prior to making the first batch, so my hat's off to him. Condolences to his friends and family.

comments.body:
I think the author often has something negative to say about China related topics, which is fine, she is prob Chinese  and has her own perspective. But I think the discussion of humanoid robots is missing an important part of the story: Japan was one of the pioneers of humanoid robotics.

Japan has decades of expertise in robotics, precision motors, sensors, actuators, and machine tools. That expertise is still highly relevant today. Even Chinese companies such as Unitree have recruited Japanese engineers and drawn on that knowledge in developing humanoid robots such as the G1.

What I find particularly interesting is the difference in how societies view these machines. The American woman in the article seems resistant to the idea of robots becoming part of everyday life. In parts of Asia, there appears to be more openness to imagining humanoid robots doing useful work, not simply dancing or demonstrating kung fu.

It's exciting to have the Michael Lewis treatment, and I even imagined who would play my favorite departed executive in the movie. What touched me most, however, is Lewis's respectful attitude toward the federal workforce and his pointing out that the American people were deliberately duped into thinking we are wastes of space by people who couldn't care less the harm it would cause to feds and those who love us. Our collective mental health was in the can for most of 2025. Recognition like this will go a long way to improving the outlook in 2026 and beyond.

comments.body: It seems to me that after succeeding in getting the Court to decide that corporations are "people", the case is an attempt to classify them as special people, i.e., immune from state lawsuits for damages they have caused.  If their argument is premised upon the Supremacy Clause, exactly what evidence is there to support a conclusion that the federal government has seen fit to occupy this area of the law.   There is simply no federal law that governs this area so these corporations are saying that since, in their view, there should be federal law on the subject, that Colorado is somehow pre-empted from the pursuit of the lawsuit in question.  I cannot even conceive of an appropriate basis for such a conclusion.
